data.title: Zemplín – a Celtic–Dacian and Slavic hillfort on the Bodrog
data.excerpt: The village of Zemplín is one of the important archaeological sites of Central Europe. The hillfort on its eastern edge was fortified in the 1st century BC by a mixed Celtic–Dacian population, later reoccupied by the Slavs and finally rebuilt into a castle of the kings of Hungary.
data.metaTitle: Zemplín – a Celtic–Dacian hillfort on the Bodrog
data.metaDescription: Zemplín on the Bodrog is a major Central European site: a Celtic–Dacian hillfort of the 1st century BC, later a Slavic hillfort and a Hungarian royal castle.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: The Hradisko rise on the eastern edge of the village, a rocky promontory at 121 m, about 1.5 km from the confluence of the Ondava and the Latorica

keyFacts.label: Dimensions of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: Oval plan of 240 × 150 m, a rampart following the edges of the elevation, about 4 m high

keyFacts.label: Construction of the rampart
keyFacts.value: In the west an earthen rampart with a core of drystone-laid stones, in the east (above the steep bank of the Bodrog) a timber palisade

keyFacts.label: The Zemplín type
keyFacts.value: The settlement structure became a model term for similar settlements in the eastern Celtic world

keyFacts.label: Crafts
keyFacts.value: Production of painted pottery (a potter's workshop with a kiln whose grate measured up to 1.8 m in diameter) and metallurgical workshops

keyFacts.label: Ethnicity
keyFacts.value: A mixed Celtic–Dacian population in the contact zone of two cultural worlds

keyFacts.label: Source
keyFacts.value: Vladimír Turčan et al.: Archeologické pamiatky – Kultúrne krásy Slovenska, Dajama, 2009

children.text: The village of Zemplín is one of the important archaeological sites of Central Europe. It lies in the southern part of the region of the same name, on the right bank of the river which, from the confluence of the Ondava with the Latorica, is for unknown reasons called the Bodrog. Its built-up area and its immediate surroundings were intensively occupied from the Neolithic onwards.

The main reason why people founded their settlements in this particular place was the good conditions for the development of agriculture and the strategically advantageous position close to the important long-distance route along the Tisza leading from south to north. One of its branches ran along the Bodrog and its tributaries towards the Carpathian passes. The earliest written source on the village, in which it is named directly as villa Zemplén, dates from 1261. It developed from an older settlement that existed in the immediate vicinity of the early feudal castle. Until the end of the 13th century the castle and the village were the property of the kings of Hungary and the centre of the Zemplín comitatus. Among the monuments that cannot be overlooked is the rise called

on the eastern edge of the village, with well-preserved rampart defences on a rocky, promontory-like elevation at 121 m above sea level. In a flat landscape with an average elevation of around 100 m the rise is a dominant landform, some one and a half kilometres from the confluence of the Ondava and the Latorica. The strategically advantageous position of the elevation gave its inhabitants natural protection from enemies and, in times of flooding, from the water of the swollen arms of the Bodrog, and from the 5th millennium BC it was repeatedly used for settlement. It was not fortified, however, until the 1st century BC. At that time a settlement complex with an ethnically mixed Celtic–Dacian population arose in the area of the present-day village. The complex consisted of a hillfort surrounded by smaller production hamlets.

The settlement structure at Zemplín, termed the Zemplín type, became a model for designating similar settlements in the eastern Celtic world. The hillfort at Zemplín, built on a rocky promontory with an oval plan and an area of 240 × 150 m, was enclosed by a rampart that followed the edges of the elevation. The construction of the defences was not uniform. The earthen rampart on the western, more easily accessible side had a core of drystone-laid stones. On the eastern side, in the stretch where the rock face dropped steeply to the Bodrog, there was only a timber palisade. The rampart is assumed to have reached a height of about four metres and to have been topped by a palisade along its crest. The main gateway into the hillfort lay on the southern side. In the eastern part of the hillfort a partly sunken building of rectangular plan was excavated, with a hearth and the typical two-post construction. The economic hinterland of the Celtic–Dacian hillfort consisted of smaller settlement units spread out in the immediate vicinity along the whole right-bank terrace of the Bodrog. Specialised craft production was also carried on in these hamlets. It chiefly involved the production of painted pottery; the area of the potters' workshops extended across the north-western part of the village, where a workshop with a large pottery kiln whose grate measured up to 1.8 m in diameter was excavated.

children.text: Metallurgical workshops were also concentrated at the hillfort. Part of the settlement agglomeration at Zemplín was a cult place lying to the south-west of the hillfort. In the La Tène period Zemplín acquired a socially and economically superior position over the nearby contemporary hamlets. The population of Zemplín was ethnically mixed, because the area lay in the contact zone between two ethnically and culturally different worlds – the Celtic and the Dacian. It experienced its period of greatest prosperity around the middle of the 1st century BC. At that time it became an important centre of the production of fine painted pottery, of metallurgy and of trade. Its importance grew beyond the bounds of the region. It acted as an intermediary for contacts between Pannonia, northern Slovakia and Lesser Poland. In the 1st century AD the Celtic–Dacian occupation of Zemplín gradually faded away and at the end of the century it came to an end under pressure from Germanic peoples advancing from the north, the bearers of the Przeworsk culture.

children.text: From the end of the 9th until the 11th century the area of the former Celtic–Dacian hillfort was used by the Slavs. They added to the older rampart defences on the eastern side and strengthened them along the whole circuit. In the 10th century, probably under the threat of attacks by Old Hungarian tribes penetrating into the Carpathian Basin, the inhabitants of the hillfort undertook an extensive rebuilding of the defences, which they raised and strengthened around the entire circuit. Pottery sherds attesting the continuity of the Slavs are found at various places in the built-up area and in the immediate surroundings of Zemplín.

Besides the dwelling from Kertalja, this is also attested by a grave of the 8th–9th century – the Great Moravian period – found in a barrow cemetery of the Roman period at Szélmalomdomb. It is certain that a larger number of people lived at Zemplín at that time, and so a more extensive cemetery must also have existed. The hillfort is mentioned in the historical romance of the so-called Anonymus from the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries. According to this mention, the place became the refuge of a Slav commander fleeing from the hillfort of Uh (today's Uzhhorod), which was being attacked by the Hungarians under the leadership of Álmos. A castle later arose on the site of the Slavic hillfort. In the 11th century the hillfort, and until the end of the 13th century the castle, belonged to the kings of Hungary. It was an important fortress on the northern frontier of the emerging Hungarian state, the seat of a župan (county governor) and the centre of the Zemplín comitatus. The last modification of the rampart probably took place at the turn of the 11th and 12th centuries, when the hillfort began to be rebuilt into a castle. A stone administrative building and probably also a church of modest size were erected.
